content: According to the 2006 book The Heartless Stone, the Kimberley Process faces two significant challenges that undermine its effectiveness. First, diamonds can be smuggled relatively easily across African borders, often accompanied by falsified histories. Second, the violent nature of diamond mining in countries not technically at war allows such diamonds to be labeled as clean, despite the ethical concerns surrounding their extraction. The Canadian government has established the Canadian Diamond Code of Conduct, a rigorous tracking system designed to authenticate Canadian diamonds and ensure their conflict-free status. This system helps maintain the integrity of Canadian diamonds in the global market. Currently, the global production of gemstones amounts to nearly 30 million carats (6,000 kg) of cut and polished stones annually. Additionally, over 100 million carats (20,000 kg) of mined diamonds are sold each year for industrial purposes, alongside approximately 100,000 kg of synthesized diamonds. The Diamond Trading Company (DTC), a subsidiary of De Beers, markets rough diamonds sourced from both De Beers mines and other mines from which it purchases production. These rough diamonds are sold to sightholders, who then cut and polish them into gemstones for sale. The cutting and polishing of rough diamonds require specialized skills and are concentrated in a few global locations, including traditional centers such as Antwerp, Amsterdam, Johannesburg, New York, and Tel Aviv. More recently, cutting centers have emerged in China, India, and Thailand. In particular, Surat in Gujarat, India, has become a hub for processing smaller carat diamonds due to its lower labor costs, while larger or more valuable diamonds are typically handled in Europe or North America. The expansion of the diamond industry in India has made it economically feasible to prepare smaller diamonds as gemstones in greater quantities. Gem-quality diamonds are sold on diamond exchanges, known as bourses, of which there are 26 registered worldwide. These exchanges represent the final tightly controlled step in the diamond supply chain. Wholesalers and retailers can purchase relatively small lots of diamonds at these bourses, after which the diamonds are prepared for final sale to consumers. Diamonds may be sold already set in jewelry or increasingly as unset (loose) stones. In 2002, the Rio Tinto Group reported that the diamonds released to the market were valued at $9 billion as rough diamonds, $14 billion after cutting and polishing, $28 billion in wholesale diamond jewelry, and $57 billion in retail sales. The Crater of Diamonds State Park in Arkansas, USA, is the only publicly accessible diamond-bearing site in the world. Located near Murfreesboro in Pike County, this state park allows visitors to search for diamonds. Natural diamonds are formed within the Earth, while synthetic diamonds are entirely manufactured. A diamond simulant is a non-diamond material designed to mimic the appearance of a diamond. These simulants, often referred to as diamante, are distinct from both natural and synthetic diamonds. The demand for diamonds in both gemological and industrial applications has driven the production of synthetic diamonds for over half a century. While industrial diamond demand has been largely met by synthetic production, recent advancements have enabled the creation of gem-quality synthetic diamonds of significant size. Most commercially available synthetic diamonds are yellow due to nitrogen impurities and are produced using High Pressure High Temperature (HPHT) processes. Other colors, such as blue, green, or pink, can be achieved by adding boron or through post-synthesis irradiation. Currently, the annual production of gem-quality synthetic diamonds is only a few thousand carats, compared to approximately 120 million carats of natural diamonds. Although the production of colorless synthetic diamonds is minimal compared to natural diamonds, fancy-colored diamonds remain rare, with only one fancy-colored diamond found for every 10,000 colorless ones. Trained gemologists can generally distinguish between natural and synthetic diamonds. Despite being theoretically identical, natural and synthetic diamonds often exhibit unique imperfections that reflect their respective origins. For example, synthetic diamonds may display specific characteristics based on their production method (HPHT or Chemical Vapor Deposition, CVD) and color. CVD diamonds can often be identified by their orange fluorescence, while D-J colored diamonds can be screened using tools like the Swiss Gemological Organization's (SSEF) Diamond Spotter or De Beers' DiamondSure UV/visible spectrometer. Natural diamonds, on the other hand, typically contain minor inclusions or flaws not present in synthetic diamonds. The origin of a truly perfect diamond, whether natural or synthetic, cannot be determined, as such diamonds are exceedingly rare. The gem quality of a diamond, which is less dependent on material properties than industrial applications, has led to the development of imitation materials and enhancement techniques. Diamond simulants, such as cubic zirconia (CZ) and moissanite, are synthetically produced materials that mimic the appearance of diamonds. While CZ is a true diamond simulant, moissanite is often marketed as a diamond replacement rather than a simulant. Enhancement techniques are applied to natural diamonds, typically those already cut and polished, to improve their gemological properties. These treatments include laser drilling to remove inclusions, the application of sealants to fill cracks, color treatments to improve a white diamond's grade, and processes to impart fancy colors to white diamonds. Trained gemologists with appropriate equipment can identify natural diamonds, simulants, and enhanced diamonds. Coatings are increasingly used to give diamond simulants, such as cubic zirconia, a more diamond-like appearance. One such material, heavily advertised, is diamond-like carbon, an amorphous carbonaceous substance with some physical properties similar to those of diamond.
